issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a statutory appeal from an arbitrator acts as a court when the appeal is directed to the High Court and is governed by its ordinary procedure.
material_facts: The compensation dispute was referred to an arbitrator, whose award was appealed to the High Court under the governing statute.
The statute provided for an appeal to the High Court, and neither the statute nor its rules prescribed a special procedure for that appeal.
The High Court determined the appeal under its ordinary rules of practice and procedure.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted as a court, not as a persona designata, and its determination was within the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction to review by special leave.
issues.legal_principle: When legislation directs an appeal to an established court without prescribing a special procedure, the court’s ordinary procedure and incidents of appeal apply. The Court relied on National Telephone Co., Ltd. v. Postmaster-General and National Sewing Thread Co., Ltd. v. James Chadwick and Bros. Ltd.; it also referred to Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. P. N. Sharma and Secretary of State for India in Council v. Chelikani Rama Rao. It rejected the contrary view in Hanskumar Kishanchand v. Union of India, distinguishing the issue there concerning whether the decision was a judgment, decree or final order from whether the High Court acted as a court.

predicates.appeal_from_arbitrator_award: A party appealed a decision made by an arbitrator.
predicates.appeal_directed_to_high_court: The governing scheme directed the appeal to the High Court itself.
predicates.ordinary_high_court_procedure_applies: No special procedure was prescribed, so the High Court determined the appeal under its ordinary procedure.

issues.definition: When an appeal from an arbitrator is directed to the High Court and governed by its ordinary procedure, the High Court acts as a court.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land cannot be determined on the basis of sale transactions that are not sufficiently contemporaneous with the acquisition or comparable to the acquired land, and a valuation resting on such evidence must be reconsidered by the fact-finding court.
material_facts: The land had been acquired nearly five years before the sale deed on which the High Court based its compensation valuation.
The arbitrator had found that land prices had risen steeply after the war, and the sale deed concerned only a small parcel.
The other sale deeds did not show sales of similar land at about the time of acquisition.
The High Court had not properly assessed the oral evidence concerning annual profits for capitalization, and the relevant revenue records for the acquisition year were not before it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s valuation based on the later sale deed could not stand. The Court set aside the decision and remitted the matter for fresh determination, allowing the parties to adduce additional evidence, including contemporaneous sale deeds and relevant revenue records.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 19(1)(e) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, compensation was measured by the land’s market value at the time of acquisition. Sale transactions must assist in determining that value by being sufficiently close in time and relating to similar land. Where the evidence does not permit a reliable valuation, the matter is for the fact-finding court to determine on proper evidence; the Supreme Court declined to reassess the evidence itself.

rule.if: land_compensation_proceeding and valuation_based_on_sale_evidence and (sale_not_contemporaneous or sale_not_comparable)

predicates.land_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerned compensation for acquired land.
predicates.valuation_based_on_sale_evidence: The court fixed compensation by relying on one or more sale transactions.
predicates.sale_not_contemporaneous: The relied-on sale took place too far from the acquisition in time to reliably indicate the land’s value at acquisition.
predicates.sale_not_comparable: The relied-on sale concerned land whose size or nature did not make it a reliable comparison to the acquired land.

issues.definition: When compensation for acquired land is based on sale evidence that is not contemporaneous or comparable, the valuation is set aside for fresh determination.

issues.legal_issue: A party need not obtain a certificate for an appeal where the challenged determination is not a judgment, decree or final order qualifying for that certificate, and the Supreme Court may excuse compliance with a procedural rule requiring an application for one.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court determination made in an appeal from an arbitrator’s award.
The Court had held that the determination was not a judgment, decree or final order for which a certificate could be sought.
The appellant asked the Court to excuse compliance with the procedural rule requiring an application for a certificate.
issues.conclusion: The certificate requirement did not apply; in any event, the Court would have excused compliance because seeking a certificate could serve no useful purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Article 133 provides for a certificate to appeal against a qualifying judgment, decree or final order of a High Court. The Court relied on Hanskumar Kishanchand v. Union of India for the conclusion that the determination at issue did not qualify. It held that the relevant requirement in Order 13, rule 2 of the Supreme Court Rules was therefore inapplicable and stated that it would have exempted the appellant from compliance even if the rule applied.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party sought to appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.challenged_decision_not_certificate_elig: The challenged decision did not qualify for a certificate-based appeal.
predicates.certificate_application_would_serve_no_p: A certificate could not be obtained for the challenged decision, making an application for one futile.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges a decision ineligible for a certificate and seeking one would be futile, compliance with a rule requiring a certificate application is excused.
